To view a copy of this licence, visit http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/ . Clear cell Carcinoma (ccRCC) is the most common and lethal subtype among renal cancers. In the present study we investigated the potential role of fatty acid-binding protein 4 (FABP4), also known as adipocyte FABP (A-FABP) or aP2 on ccRCC progression. Firstly, we found that FABP4 median serum levels were significantly higher in ccRCC patients compared to HD. Based on this result and to evaluate whether FABP4 plays a role on renal cancer malignant phenotype, we analyzed proliferation and migration in 786-O and ACHN cell lines using recombinant FABP4. We found that FABP4 significantly increased cell migration, whereas it had no significant effect on proliferation. As FABP4 is mainly expressed by adipocytes, we measured FABP4 adipocyte conditioned media (Ad-CM) levels showing that Ad-CM from ccRCC (Ad-CM ccRCC) had significantly higher mean values compared to Ad-CM obtained from Healthy Donors (HD). To assess the effects of adipocyte-released FABP-4, on cancer malignant phenotype we evaluated 786-O and ACHN proliferation and migration, using Ad-CM from ccRCC and Ad-CM from HD alone or in combination with FABP4 inhibitor BMS309403. Our results showed that Ad-CM enhanced cell proliferation in ACHN, but not in 786-O and on cell motility in both cell lines and this effect was partially reverted by BMS309403 in both cell lines. Moreover, in both cell lines, FABP4 effect was associated with an increased ERK phosphorylation. Collectively these data support the role of FABP4 in ccRCC progression and its potential use as noninvasive biomarker and therapeutic target for ccRCC. Keywords Adipocytes Renal cancer Peri-renal adipose tissue FABP4 issue-copyright-statement © BioMed Central Ltd., part of Springer Nature 2025 Introduction Renal carcinoma includes a heterogeneous group of malignancies from renal tubular epithelial cells that account for about 2.2% of all tumors and 1.8% of the total cancer mortality worldwide [ 1 ]. Generally, less than 10% of patients with RCC are diagnosed with the classic triad of flank pain, hematuria and palpable mass, more often the diagnosis occurs as incidental findings during ultrasonography or abdominal CT performed for another reason [ 2 ]. Accordingly, about 25% of patients present with distant metastatic disease at diagnosis [ 3 ]. Early detection of organ-confined RCC allows curative surgical resection via partial or radical nephrectomy and about 30% of patient who undergo surgical resection develop recurrence associated with high mortality rate [ 4 ]. Clear cell Renal Cell Carcinoma (ccRCC) is the most common and lethal subtype among renal cancers, comprising almost the 70% of cases [ 5 ]. Several epidemiological studies reported a strong association between perirenal adipose tissue (PRAT) thickness measured by computer tomography scan and ccRCC histotype in patients with renal cortical tumor [ 6 ]. In addition, it has been reported that PRAT width is associated with poor Progression Free Survival (PFS) [ 7 ] and Overall Survival (OS) in patients with surgical treated ccRCC [ 8 ]. These epidemiological data suggest that Peri-Renal Adipose Tissue (PRAT) may affect ccRCC behavior through the exchange of proteins, cytokines and metabolites with cancer cells [ 9 ], thanks to an extensive network of blood and lymph vessels connecting PRAT and ccRCC [ 10 ]. PRAT, in fact, is a peculiar visceral fat depot, defined along with pericardial Adipose Tissue (AT) and renal sinus fat an “ectopic fat” [ 11 ]. It is able to regulate kidney homeostasis in physiological conditions and involved in different metabolic diseases such as hypertension, atherosclerosis, and insulin resistance [ 12 ]. Thus, it is possible to speculate that peri-renal mature adipocytes may exert their effect on tumor microenvironment through secretion of adipokines and/or growth factors that support tumor progression. Although it is well known that high perirenal fat accumulation is associated with increased mortality and poor PFS of patients with localized ccRCC [ 7 , 8 ], the molecular mechanism underlying the relationship between perirenal adipocytes and ccRCC spread is still unclear. The discovery of extracellular FABP4 (e-FABP4) as adipocyte-released factor changed the game in research of a mechanistic link between cancer and AT. This small protein of 15 kDa is a fatty acid carrier, secreted by adipocytes, macrophages and endothelial cells, it is involved in metabolic disorders associated to visceral adiposity such as insulin resistance and atherosclerosis. Interestingly, e-FABP4 has been identified as driver of cell proliferation and migration in breast [ 13 ], colon [ 14 ], and ovarian cancer [ 15 ]. In the present study, we investigated the effect of FABP4 and adipocyte-released FABP4 on ccRCC cell proliferation and migration.

extracted_data.document_summary: This study investigates the role of fatty acid-binding protein 4 (FABP4), particularly adipocyte-released e-FABP4, in clear cell Renal Cell Carcinoma (ccRCC) progression and its correlation with peri-renal adipose tissue. It demonstrates that FABP4 serum levels and e-FABP4 in adipocyte conditioned media are significantly higher in ccRCC patients. In vitro experiments showed that recombinant FABP4 significantly promotes ccRCC cell migration and ERK phosphorylation, while adipocyte-released factors (other than FABP4) also enhance ACHN cell proliferation. These findings highlight FABP4 as a driver of ccRCC progression and a potential noninvasive biomarker and therapeutic target.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Investigation of FABP4's role in renal cancer progression through in vitro studies using recombinant FABP4, adipocyte-conditioned media (Ad-CM) from ccRCC patients and healthy donors, and the FABP4 inhibitor BMS309403, alongside analysis of patient serum biomarkers.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: In vitro experiments involved recombinant FABP4 (specifically at 10000 pg/mL), Adipocyte-Conditioned Medium (Ad-CM) from ccRCC patients and healthy donors, and the FABP4 inhibitor BMS309403. Cells were treated for proliferation and migration assays, with Mitomycin C (10 µg/mL) used to halt proliferation in scratch assays. While specific concentrations were provided for some reagents, comprehensive dose-response comparisons were generally not reported. Patient serum FABP4 levels were also compared between ccRCC patients and healthy donors.

analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Blood Serum, Adipocyte Conditioned Media (Ad-CM) from peri-renal adipose tissue, 786-O and ACHN renal cancer cell lines
analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Protein level, Secretion, Effect on cell migration and proliferation

measured_effect.direction_of_change: higher (serum, Ad-CM), increased (cell migration), unchanged (proliferation in 786-O and ACHN by recombinant FABP4 alone)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification:
FABP4 median serum levels were significantly higher in ccRCC patients [18680 pg/mL (IQ: 24930-13388)] compared to Healthy Donors [14090 pg/mL (IQ: 18733-11288)] (p=0.0292). Ad-CM from ccRCC patients had a significantly higher mean e-FABP4 concentration [10150 pg/mL 
± 3835] compared to Ad-CM from Healthy Donors [5578 pg/mL 
± 2969] (p=0.0048). Recombinant FABP4 (10000 pg/mL) significantly increased cell migration in 786-O and ACHN cells. FABP4 treatment (10000 pg/mL) had no significant effect on cell proliferation in 786-O (p=0.061) and ACHN (p=0.995) cells.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Fatty acid carrier and binding protein, highly expressed in adipocytes, involved in metabolic disorders, inflammation, acts as a lipid chaperone and free fatty acid transporter. Identified as a driver of cell proliferation and migration in various cancers.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: ccRCC progression, presence in ccRCC patients, crosstalk between peri-renal adipose tissue and ccRCC, adipocyte-released factors promoting cancer aggressiveness, in vitro studies on 786-O and ACHN renal cancer cell lines, and inhibition by BMS309403.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Potential noninvasive biomarker and therapeutic target for ccRCC, associated with ccRCC progression and malignant phenotype, a driver of adipose tissue cancer-promoting effect, and indicates enhanced ccRCC cell motility and spread.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: FABP4 effect was associated with an increased ERK phosphorylation. Both Ad-CM from ccRCC and recombinant FABP4 treatment significantly increased ERK phosphorylation. FABP4 inhibitor mitigated ERK phosphorylation induced by Ad-CM from ccRCC and recombinant FABP4 in both cell lines. Quantitative statistical data not provided beyond qualitative description of significance.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Key signaling event and crucial transducer of extracellular signals, regulating cellular processes such as proliferation, differentiation, cell shape, and motility; involved in coordinating cell movement, and plays a pivotal role in extracellular FABP4 signaling.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: FABP4 effect in 786-O and ACHN renal cancer cell lines, activation by Ad-CM from ccRCC, and mitigation by FABP4 inhibitor, mediating enhanced motility of ccRCC cells.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Associated with FABP4-mediated cell migration and progression of ccRCC, indicates increased ccRCC cell motility and metastatic spread, a key factor in cancer progression.

analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: ACHN ccRCC cell line, 786-O and ACHN ccRCC cell lines
analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Effect on cell proliferation, Effect on cell migration

measured_effect.direction_of_change: higher (proliferation in ACHN), higher (migration in both cell lines)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Ad-CM from both HD and ccRCC enhanced cell proliferation in ACHN (p=0.0039 and p=0.0089, respectively). This effect on proliferation was not reverted by BMS309403. Ad-CM from ccRCC enhanced cell migration in both 786-O and ACHN; this effect was partially reverted by BMS309403, indicating e-FABP4 is one of the drivers. Quantitative statistical data for migration not provided beyond qualitative description.
